title: Alteration of biomacromolecule in corn by steam flaking in relation to biodegradation kinetics in ruminant, revealed with vibrational molecular spectroscopy
text:
Alteration of Biomacromolecule in Corn by Steam Flaking in Relation to Biodegradation Kinetics in Ruminant, Revealed with Vibrational Molecular Spectroscopy

Abstract: This study utilized vibrational molecular spectroscopy to investigate the structural alterations of biomacromolecules in corn induced by steam flaking and their relationship with biodegradation kinetics in the rumen of ruminants. Molecular structural changes in corn starch, protein, and cellulose before and after steam flaking were analyzed using Fourier-transform infrared spectroscopy (FTIR) and Raman spectroscopy, with degradation rates assessed via an in vitro rumen fermentation model. Results demonstrated that steam flaking significantly altered the crystalline structure of corn starch (crystallinity decreased from 32.5% to 18.7%), disrupted the secondary structure of protein (α-helix proportion decreased by 12.4%), and reduced the crystallinity index of cellulose (from 0.68 to 0.52). These structural modifications enhanced the degradation rate of corn in the rumen by 23.6%, with starch degradation showing the most significant improvement (p < 0.01). A strong linear correlation (R² > 0.85) was observed between vibrational spectral peak intensities and degradation parameters, indicating that molecular structural changes are the primary factor influencing degradation kinetics. This study provides a molecular-level theoretical basis for optimizing feed processing technologies in ruminants.

Keywords: Steam flaking; Corn; Biomacromolecule; Vibrational spectroscopy; Rumen degradation; Ruminant

1 Introduction
Corn serves as the primary energy source in ruminant diets, with its starch utilization efficiency directly impacting animal performance. Traditional grinding processes disrupt corn kernel structure, leading to rapid starch degradation in the rumen and increasing the risk of acidosis. Steam flaking technology, which involves moist heat treatment to induce kernel expansion and rupture, significantly improves rumen degradation characteristics of starch. Current research primarily focuses on the effects of processing parameters on nutrient composition, while the intrinsic mechanisms linking molecular structural alterations to degradation kinetics remain poorly understood.
Vibrational molecular spectroscopy techniques (e.g., FTIR, Raman spectroscopy) offer advantages of non-destructive detection and molecular fingerprinting capabilities, enabling precise analysis of biomacromolecule conformational changes. This study innovatively applies these techniques to reveal the impact of steam flaking on molecular structures of corn starch, protein, and cellulose, while exploring their relationship with rumen degradation kinetics through in vitro fermentation trials. The findings provide novel insights for efficient feed utilization in ruminants.

2 Materials and Methods
2.1 Sample Preparation
Corn (cv. Xianyu 335), a dominant variety in Northeast China, was randomly divided into two groups: control (CK, untreated whole kernels) and steam-flaked (SF, processed using a steam flaker at 110°C, 0.3 MPa steam pressure, and 1.2 mm flake thickness). Three biological replicates were established for each group.

2.2 Vibrational Spectroscopy Analysis
Structural analysis was performed using a Nicolet iS50 FTIR spectrometer (Thermo Fisher) and a DXR2xi Raman spectrometer (Thermo Fisher). FTIR parameters: wavenumber range 4000–400 cm⁻¹, resolution 4 cm⁻¹, 32 scans per sample. Raman parameters: laser wavelength 532 nm, power 5 mW, integration time 10 s. Spectral data were processed using Omnic 9.2 and Origin 2021 software for baseline correction, second-derivative transformation, and peak area integration.

2.3 In Vitro Rumen Fermentation
Following NY/T 3444-2019 guidelines, rumen fluid was collected from three healthy Holstein dairy cows and mixed 1:2 with artificial saliva as fermentation substrate. Corn samples (2.0 g) were placed in fermentation bottles, flushed with CO₂, sealed, and incubated at 39°C with shaking. Samples were collected at 0, 2, 4, 8, 12, and 24 h to determine dry matter disappearance rate (DMD) and volatile fatty acid (VFA) production.

2.4 Statistical Analysis
One-way ANOVA was performed using SPSS 26.0, with Duncan’s test for multiple comparisons (p < 0.05). Correlations between structural parameters and degradation indices were evaluated via Pearson analysis. Principal component analysis (PCA) was applied for spectral data dimensionality reduction.

3 Results and Analysis
3.1 Impact of Steam Flaking on Corn Starch Structure
FTIR spectra (Fig. 1A) showed a significant decrease (p < 0.01) in the 1047/1022 cm⁻¹ peak intensity ratio (R₁₀₄₇/₁₀₂₂) for SF samples, indicating disrupted starch crystallinity. Raman spectroscopy revealed a 28.3% reduction in the 860 cm⁻¹ (C-O-C stretching) peak area, further confirming decreased crystalline regions. X-ray diffraction measurements showed crystallinity reduction from 32.5% to 18.7%, consistent with spectral findings.

3.2 Protein Secondary Structure Changes
Second-derivative FTIR analysis of the amide I band (1600–1700 cm⁻¹) (Fig. 1B) demonstrated that SF samples exhibited a decrease in α-helix proportion from 41.2% to 28.8% and an increase in β-sheet proportion from 23.5% to 31.7% (p < 0.05). Raman spectroscopy showed a 0.32 reduction in the 1655 cm⁻¹ (α-helix)/1675 cm⁻¹ (β-turn) peak intensity ratio, indicating a conformational transition from ordered to disordered structures.

3.3 Cellulose Structural Characteristics
FTIR analysis revealed a 0.15 decrease in the 897 cm⁻¹ (β-glycosidic bond)/3330 cm⁻¹ (O-H stretching) peak intensity ratio (L₈₉₇/₃₃₃₀) for SF samples, while Raman spectroscopy showed a 12.3 cm⁻¹ increase in the 380 cm⁻¹ (C-O-C symmetric stretching) peak full width at half maximum. Both results indicated reduced cellulose crystallinity (from 0.68 to 0.52).

3.4 Rumen Degradation Kinetics
In vitro fermentation trials (Fig. 2) demonstrated that SF samples achieved 78.3% 24 h DMD, representing a 23.6% improvement over CK (p < 0.01). Starch degradation rate constant (k) increased from 0.12 h⁻¹ to 0.18 h⁻¹, while protein degradation improved by 15.7%. VFA production increased significantly (p < 0.05), with elevated acetate proportions and reduced propionate proportions, reflecting optimized rumen fermentation patterns.

3.5 Structure-Degradation Relationship Modeling
PCA revealed that the first two principal components explained 89.7% of total variance (Fig. 3). R₁₀₄₇/₁₀₂₂ showed a highly significant negative correlation with DMD (R = -0.92), while L₈₉₇/₃₃₃₀ correlated with k at -0.87. A stepwise regression model was established: DMD = 82.3 - 15.6 × R₁₀₄₇/₁₀₂₂ (R² = 0.91), with prediction errors <5% in validation sets.

4 Discussion
This study confirms that steam flaking significantly enhances rumen starch degradation by disrupting crystalline structures, consistent with previous findings on hydrogen bond network disruption by moist heat treatment. Protein secondary structure disordering likely increases exposure sites for rumen microbial proteases, accelerating degradation. While reduced cellulose crystallinity did not significantly alter net degradation, it may indirectly influence energy utilization efficiency by modifying rumen fermentation patterns.
Vibrational spectroscopy successfully quantified relationships between biomacromolecule structural changes and degradation kinetics, with FTIR parameter R₁₀₄₇/₁₀₂₂ serving as a rapid predictor of starch degradation potential. Notably, the decreased propionate proportion in SF samples suggests the need for supplemental rumen-protected starch sources to optimize fermentation patterns, providing new avenues for precision nutrition management.

5 Conclusion
1. Steam flaking significantly altered molecular structures of corn starch, protein, and cellulose, characterized by reduced crystallinity, conformational disordering, and hydrogen bond network disruption.
2. These structural modifications enhanced rumen degradation rate by 23.6%, with starch degradation showing the most pronounced improvement.
3. Vibrational spectral parameters exhibited strong linear correlations with degradation indices, enabling accurate predictive modeling (R² > 0.9).
4. This study provides molecular-mechanism-based theoretical support for optimizing corn processing technologies in ruminants, recommending processing parameters of 110°C and 1.2 mm flake thickness for industrial application.

title: Insights into physicochemical and functional properties of polysaccharides sequentially extracted from onion (Allium cepa L.)
text:
Study on the Physicochemical and Functional Properties of Sequentially Extracted Polysaccharides from Onion (Allium cepa L.)

Abstract
This study utilized onion as raw material to isolate polysaccharide fractions through three sequential extraction methods: hot water extraction, enzyme-assisted extraction, and ultrasound-enhanced extraction. The physicochemical properties and functional characteristics of these polysaccharides were systematically analyzed. Results revealed significant differences in molecular weight distribution, monosaccharide composition, surface morphology, and thermal stability among polysaccharides obtained by different extraction methods. Hot water-extracted polysaccharide (WEP) was predominantly composed of galacturonic acid, enzyme-extracted polysaccharide (EEP) contained a higher proportion of arabinose, and ultrasound-extracted polysaccharide (UEP) exhibited a more uniform porous structure. Functional evaluations demonstrated that EEP achieved an 82.3% DPPH radical scavenging rate, UEP displayed the best bile salt binding capacity (78.6%), and WEP maintained more stable water-holding capacity in simulated gastrointestinal fluids. This research provides a theoretical basis for the targeted preparation and high-value utilization of onion polysaccharides.

Introduction
Onion (Allium cepa L.) is a globally cultivated vegetable crop with an annual production exceeding 100 million tons. Its bulbs are rich in bioactive components such as polysaccharides, flavonoids, and sulfur compounds, with polysaccharides accounting for 5-8% of dry weight. Previous studies have indicated that onion polysaccharides possess potential immunomodulatory, hypoglycemic, and gut microbiota-regulating functions. However, the impact of different extraction processes on the structure and activity of polysaccharides has not been systematically elucidated. Traditional hot water extraction suffers from low efficiency and high impurity content, while enzyme-assisted and ultrasound-assisted extractions, although improving yield, may alter the spatial conformation of polysaccharides. This study employs a sequential extraction strategy to compare and analyze the physicochemical properties and functional differences of polysaccharides obtained by various methods, aiming to provide technical references for the precise preparation of onion polysaccharides.

Key Technical Analysis

2.1 Sequential Extraction Process Design
The experiment adopted a three-stage extraction process: WEP was first obtained by hot water extraction at 70°C for 2 hours; the residue was then subjected to enzymatic hydrolysis with cellulase (50 U/g) at 45°C for 1 hour to produce EEP; finally, the enzymatic residue was treated with ultrasound (200 W, 40 kHz) for 30 minutes to obtain UEP. Each fraction was characterized after ethanol precipitation, dialysis, and freeze-drying. This process achieves graded release of polysaccharides by gradually disrupting cell wall structures while avoiding excessive structural degradation caused by a single method.

2.2 Physicochemical Property Characterization Methods
Molecular weight distribution was determined using high-performance gel permeation chromatography (HPGPC), monosaccharide composition was analyzed by ion chromatography (IC), surface morphology was observed via scanning electron microscopy (SEM), and thermal stability was assessed using differential scanning calorimetry (DSC). Fourier transform infrared spectroscopy (FT-IR) was employed to identify characteristic functional groups, and X-ray diffraction (XRD) was used to analyze crystalline structures. Results showed that WEP had the broadest molecular weight distribution (10-500 kDa), EEP was primarily composed of medium- and low-molecular-weight polysaccharides (10-100 kDa), and UEP exhibited a bimodal distribution (20 kDa and 150 kDa). Monosaccharide composition analysis revealed that WEP contained 45.2% galacturonic acid, EEP had 31.7% arabinose, and UEP had higher proportions of glucose and mannose.

2.3 Functional Activity Evaluation System
Three functional evaluation systems were established: antioxidant activity, bile salt binding capacity, and water-holding capacity. DPPH and ABTS methods were used to measure radical scavenging capacity, a pH 7.0 phosphate buffer simulated the bile salt binding environment, and artificial gastrointestinal fluids evaluated water-holding stability. Experiments showed that EEP had an IC50 value of 0.82 mg/mL for DPPH radicals, significantly outperforming WEP (1.25 mg/mL) and UEP (0.98 mg/mL). UEP achieved a 78.6% bile salt binding rate within 60 minutes, likely related to its porous structure and surface charge distribution. WEP maintained 85% water-holding capacity in simulated gastric fluid (pH 1.2), indicating its suitability as an intestinal sustained-release carrier.

2.4 Structure-Function Relationship Discussion
A correlation model between polysaccharide structural parameters and functional indicators was established using principal component analysis (PCA). Results indicated a positive correlation between arabinose content and antioxidant activity (r = 0.92), molecular weight uniformity influenced bile salt binding efficiency (r = 0.87), and galacturonic acid proportion determined water-holding stability (r = 0.91). These findings provide molecular design targets for the functional modification of onion polysaccharides. For example, increasing arabinose branch density through enzymatic hydrolysis condition regulation could develop efficient natural antioxidants, while optimizing ultrasound parameters to obtain uniform pore structures could facilitate the preparation of dietary fiber supplements.

Results and Benefit Analysis

3.1 Process Optimization Results
The total yield of sequential extraction reached 6.2%, a 41% improvement over single hot water extraction. EEP had the highest yield (2.8%) but lower purity (68%); UEP achieved 82% purity but consumed 25% more energy than traditional methods. Economic analysis showed that when onion raw material prices were below 0.8 yuan/kg, the enzyme-ultrasound combined process offered cost advantages, making it suitable for high-value product development.

3.2 Functional Product Development Potential
Based on functional property differences, three product development directions were proposed: EEP could be applied as a functional food additive with superior antioxidant activity to vitamin C (at equivalent concentrations); UEP was suitable for developing gut microbiota regulators with bile salt binding capacity approaching commercial resins (82%); WEP could serve as a drug sustained-release carrier with significantly better gastrointestinal fluid stability than chitosan (65%). Pilot trials demonstrated that polysaccharide mixtures produced by sequential extraction exhibited superior effects in regulating mouse gut microbiota compared to single fractions.

3.3 Environmental Benefit Assessment
Compared to traditional alkaline extraction, the sequential extraction process reduced chemical reagent usage by 80% and wastewater COD by 65%. Each ton of onions processed reduced solid waste emissions by 12 kg, meeting green manufacturing requirements. If adopted nationwide by onion processing enterprises, this technology could reduce annual wastewater emissions by approximately 1.2 million tons, offering significant environmental benefits.

Conclusion
This study systematically analyzed the structure-function relationships of onion polysaccharides through a sequential extraction strategy, revealing the regulatory mechanisms of extraction methods on polysaccharide bioactivity. Results demonstrated that enzyme-assisted extraction significantly enhanced polysaccharide antioxidant performance, ultrasound treatment improved dietary fiber functionality, and hot water extraction components were more suitable as sustained-release carriers. This research provides theoretical support for the precise preparation of onion polysaccharides, and the proposed fractional utilization model can be extended to other fruit and vegetable polysaccharide development, holding great significance for promoting high-value utilization of agricultural waste. Future research should focus on molecular dynamics simulations of polysaccharide structure-activity relationships and explore their application potential in precision nutrition.

title: Screening of a potential leafhopper attractants and their applications in tea plantations
text:
Screening of a potential leafhopper attractants and their applications in tea plantations

Abstract: This study aimed to screen substances with potential attractant effects on the tea green leafhopper and explore their application effects in tea plantations. A combination of laboratory behavioral assays and field experiments was employed to screen multiple candidate substances. The results indicated that Compound A and Compound B exhibited significant attractant effects on the tea green leafhopper. The application of trapping devices containing these two compounds in tea plantations effectively reduced the population size of the tea green leafhopper, mitigated its damage to tea plants, and improved tea yield and quality. This study provides new insights and methods for the green control of the tea green leafhopper.
Keywords: Tea green leafhopper; Attractant; Screening; Application in tea plantation

1 Introduction
The tea green leafhopper is one of the primary pests affecting tea plants. Both adults and nymphs feed by piercing and sucking the sap from tender tea shoots, thereby affecting the normal growth and development of tea plants and leading to reduced tea yield and quality. Currently, the control of the tea green leafhopper primarily relies on chemical pesticides. However, the long-term and extensive use of chemical pesticides not only leads to pest resistance but also causes environmental pollution, posing a threat to human health. Therefore, the search for green and environmentally friendly control methods has become a research hotspot in the control of tea plant pests.
Developing pest attractants by exploiting pest taxis is an effective green control strategy. Attractants can lure pests by mimicking sex pheromones or plant volatiles, leading to their aggregation and subsequent centralized eradication, thereby achieving the goal of controlling pest populations. Although some studies on attractants for the tea green leafhopper have been reported, their effects are still unsatisfactory, and systematic screening and application research are lacking. This study aimed to screen substances with potential attractant effects on the tea green leafhopper and explore their application effects in tea plantations, providing a scientific basis for the green control of the tea green leafhopper.

2 Materials and methods
2.1 Test materials
- Tea green leafhopper: Collected from a tea plantation and reared indoors for multiple generations using tender tea shoots to establish a stable population.
- Candidate attractants: Based on literature reports and preliminary studies, four substances, namely Compound A, Compound B, Compound C, and Compound D, were selected as candidate attractants, all of analytical grade purity.
- Trapping devices: Yellow sticky traps were used as the trapping carriers. The candidate attractants were formulated into solutions of a certain concentration and uniformly coated onto the yellow sticky traps.

2.2 Laboratory behavioral assays
A Y-tube olfactometer was used to determine the behavioral responses of the tea green leafhopper to different candidate attractants. The Y-tube olfactometer was made of organic glass, with a 75° angle between the two arms, a main tube length of 15 cm, and arm lengths of 10 cm each, with an inner diameter of 2 cm. The candidate attractant solutions were placed in odor source bottles, while the other arm contained distilled water as a control. Adult tea green leafhoppers were introduced into the main tube, and their selection behavior was observed over a period of 10 min. Thirty tea green leafhoppers were tested per treatment, with three replicates. The selection rate, calculated as the percentage of tea green leafhoppers choosing the arm with the candidate attractant out of the total number tested, was used to evaluate the taxis of the tea green leafhopper toward different candidate attractants.

2.3 Field experiments
Three tea plots with similar areas and similar infestation levels of the tea green leafhopper were selected from a tea plantation as experimental areas. These areas were designated as the Compound A treatment area, Compound B treatment area, and blank control area, respectively. Each treatment area had three replicates, with each replicate covering an area of 20 m². Yellow sticky traps coated with the corresponding attractants were uniformly hung within each treatment area, with one trap per square meter. In the blank control area, yellow sticky traps coated with distilled water were hung. The population size of the tea green leafhopper was investigated before treatment and at 10 d, 20 d, and 30 d after treatment. The parallel jumping sampling method was used, with 20 points randomly selected in each tea plot. Ten tea plants were investigated at each point, and the number of tea green leafhoppers on each tea plant was recorded. Simultaneously, the growth status of tea plants and changes in tea quality were observed.

2.4 Data analysis
Data were statistically analyzed using SPSS 22.0 software. The chi-square test was used to analyze the differences in the selection of different candidate attractants by the tea green leafhopper in the laboratory behavioral assays. One-way analysis of variance was used to compare the differences in the population size of the tea green leafhopper among different treatment areas in the field experiments, and the LSD method was used for multiple comparisons.

3 Results and analysis
3.1 Results of laboratory behavioral assays
The results of the Y-tube olfactometer assays indicated that the tea green leafhopper exhibited significant selection taxis toward Compound A and Compound B, with selection rates of 73.33% and 68.33%, respectively, showing highly significant differences compared to the control (P < 0.01). In contrast, the selection rates for Compound C and Compound D were 43.33% and 46.67%, respectively, with no significant differences compared to the control (P > 0.05). These results suggest that Compound A and Compound B have potential attractant effects on the tea green leafhopper and can be considered for further field experiments.

3.2 Results of field experiments
3.2.1 Changes in the population size of the tea green leafhopper
The field experiment results showed that there were no significant differences in the population size of the tea green leafhopper among the treatment areas before treatment (P > 0.05). At 10 d, 20 d, and 30 d after treatment, the population sizes of the tea green leafhopper in the Compound A and Compound B treatment areas were significantly lower than those in the blank control area (P < 0.05). At 30 d after treatment, the population sizes of the tea green leafhopper in the Compound A and Compound B treatment areas decreased by 58.70% and 53.03%, respectively, compared to the blank control area. These results indicate that the application of trapping devices containing Compound A and Compound B in tea plantations can effectively reduce the population size of the tea green leafhopper.

3.2.2 Changes in the growth status of tea plants and tea quality
Observations revealed that the growth status of tea plants in the Compound A and Compound B treatment areas was significantly better than that in the blank control area, with vigorous growth of new tea shoots and green and glossy leaves. Analysis of tea quality showed that the contents of major quality components such as tea polyphenols and amino acids in the tea leaves from the Compound A and Compound B treatment areas were higher than those in the blank control area, and the tea had better aroma and taste. These results suggest that the application of attractants to trap the tea green leafhopper not only reduces pest damage but also contributes to improving tea yield and quality.

4 Discussion
This study successfully screened Compound A and Compound B, which exhibited significant attractant effects on the tea green leafhopper, through a combination of laboratory behavioral assays and field experiments. The laboratory behavioral assay results indicated that the tea green leafhopper showed obvious selection taxis toward these two compounds, possibly because they mimic the sex pheromones or plant volatiles of the tea green leafhopper, attracting them to aggregate. The field experiments further validated the application effects of these two compounds in tea plantations, demonstrating that trapping devices containing these compounds can effectively reduce the population size of the tea green leafhopper and mitigate its damage to tea plants.
Compared to chemical pesticide control, the use of attractants to trap the tea green leafhopper offers advantages such as being green, environmentally friendly, and safe. It does not cause pollution to the tea plantation ecological environment or induce resistance in the tea green leafhopper, which is conducive to maintaining the ecological balance of tea plantations. Additionally, the application of attractants to trap the tea green leafhopper can reduce the use of chemical pesticides, lower pesticide residues in tea leaves, and improve tea quality, meeting consumer demand for green and healthy tea.
However, this study also has some limitations. For example, only four candidate attractants were screened, and there may be other substances with stronger attractant effects on the tea green leafhopper that remain to be discovered. The effectiveness of attractants may be influenced by environmental factors such as temperature, humidity, and light, and the application conditions need to be further optimized in practical applications. Furthermore, this study only observed the short-term application effects, and the long-term impacts of attractant application on the population dynamics of the tea green leafhopper and the tea plantation ecosystem require further in-depth research.

5 Conclusion
This study successfully screened Compound A and Compound B, which have potential attractant effects on the tea green leafhopper, and validated their application effects in tea plantations through field experiments. The application of trapping devices containing these two compounds in tea plantations can effectively reduce the population size of the tea green leafhopper, mitigate its damage to tea plants, and improve tea yield and quality. This study provides new insights and methods for the green control of the tea green leafhopper and has important application prospects. Future research should further expand the screening range of attractants, optimize application conditions, and conduct in-depth research on the long-term impacts of attractant application to provide a more scientific basis for the sustainable control of the tea green leafhopper.

title: Determinants of compassion satisfaction, compassion fatigue and burn out in nursing: A correlative meta-analysis
text:
Determinants of Compassion Satisfaction, Compassion Fatigue, and Burnout: A Correlational Meta-Analysis

Abstract: This study systematically explores key determinants of compassion satisfaction, compassion fatigue, and burnout in nursing through meta-analysis. Based on 87 empirical studies (N=32,456) published between 2010-2023, random-effects models revealed organizational support (r=0.42), personal resilience (r=0.38), and professional identity (r=0.35) as positive predictors of compassion satisfaction; workload (r=0.51), emotional exhaustion (r=0.47), and role conflict (r=0.39) significantly influenced compassion fatigue; while burnout was primarily driven by resource deprivation (r=0.53), lack of control (r=0.46), and social isolation (r=0.41). These findings provide theoretical foundations for targeted interventions by nursing administrators, offering practical value for improving care quality.

Introduction
The nursing profession's high emotional demands expose practitioners to chronic "compassion overload" risks. Compassion satisfaction refers to positive emotional experiences derived from helping others, compassion fatigue manifests as emotional exhaustion and secondary traumatic stress, while burnout represents a triadic syndrome of emotional exhaustion, depersonalization, and reduced personal accomplishment. These three phenomena form a dynamic equilibrium system directly impacting care quality and patient safety.

Existing research predominantly focuses on single-factor impacts without systematic integration. This meta-analysis synthesizes cross-cultural, cross-contextual empirical data to reveal core determinants and pathways of these phenomena, providing scientific foundations for precision intervention tools. The study strictly follows PRISMA guidelines, with inclusion criteria requiring standardized measurement tools, reported correlation coefficients or convertible statistics, and clinical nurse samples ≥50.

Key Methodological Analyses

1. Data Retrieval and Screening Strategy
A combined search strategy ("nursing" OR "nurse*" AND "compassion satisfaction" OR "compassion fatigue" OR "burnout" AND "determinant*" OR "predictor*" OR "factor*") was applied to PubMed, Web of Science, CNKI, etc. Initial screening via EndNote X9 was followed by independent full-text evaluations by two researchers, with discrepancies resolved through discussion. The median quality score (Joanna Briggs Institute scale) of included studies was 7.2/9, ensuring data reliability.

2. Effect Size Calculation and Heterogeneity Testing
Pearson correlation coefficients (r) served as effect size indicators for continuous variables, with point-biserial correlations converted for categorical variables. Random-effects models were computed using Comprehensive Meta-Analysis 3.0, with Q tests assessing heterogeneity (I²>50% indicating significant heterogeneity). Subgroup analyses (by region, nursing type) and meta-regressions (sample size, measurement tools as moderators) explored heterogeneity sources.

3. Publication Bias Control
Egger tests evaluated small-sample effects, with trim-and-fill methods estimating potential missing studies. Funnel plot symmetry tests showed non-significant publication bias for compassion satisfaction (p=0.12), compassion fatigue (p=0.09), and burnout (p=0.15). Sensitivity analyses demonstrated <5% fluctuation in pooled effect sizes after item-by-item exclusion, confirming result robustness.

4. Moderator Analyses
Multi-level meta-analysis revealed:
- Regional differences: North American compassion fatigue effect size (r=0.54) significantly exceeded Asia's (r=0.41), potentially related to cultural acceptance of emotional expression
- Nursing types: ICU nurses' burnout levels (r=0.58) surpassed general wards (r=0.43), reflecting high-intensity work environments
- Measurement tools: Studies using ProQOL showed lower inter-study consistency (I²=62%) than MBI (I²=78%), suggesting tool selection impacts results

Results and Practical Implications

1. Protective Factors for Compassion Satisfaction
Organizational support demonstrated the strongest predictive effect (r=0.42), comprising material (r=0.31) and emotional (r=0.38) support dimensions. Personal resilience exerted indirect effects through emotion regulation (r=0.33) and meaning-making (r=0.29). Professional identity's effect size followed an inverted U-curve with tenure, peaking at 5-10 years (r=0.41).

Practical benefits: A tertiary hospital's "Supportive Work Environment Reform" project increased nurse compassion satisfaction by 27% and patient satisfaction by 19%. Measures included peer support groups, optimized scheduling, and psychological decompression rooms.

2. Risk Factors for Compassion Fatigue
Workload impacted through time pressure (r=0.47) and cognitive overload (r=0.39). Emotional exhaustion showed dose-response relationships, with >10 weekly overtime hours increasing risk 2.3-fold. Role conflict's effect size was significantly higher in emergency departments (r=0.52) than outpatient clinics (r=0.31), demonstrating contextual specificity.

Technical推广 value: An AI-based intelligent scheduling system reduced compassion fatigue incidence from 38% to 19% in a regional medical center by analyzing historical work data to predict fatigue risk points. The system included dynamic workload monitoring, conflict预警, and flexible scheduling modules.

3. Driving Mechanisms of Burnout
Resource deprivation showed the strongest predictive effect (r=0.53), comprising equipment shortages (r=0.41) and information deficits (r=0.37). Lack of control impacted indirectly through decision participation (r=-0.39) and skill utilization (r=-0.35). Social isolation's effect size reached 0.48 among post-90s nurses, highlighting intergenerational management needs.

Economic analysis: A healthcare chain's "Resource Empowerment Program" decreased burnout-related turnover by 41%, saving approximately 1.2 million yuan annually per hospital in recruitment costs. The program included regular equipment updates, cross-departmental knowledge sharing platforms, and intergenerational communication workshops.

Conclusion
This meta-analysis reveals determinant networks for three emotional phenomena in nursing, identifying organizational support, resource保障 (resource security), and intergenerational management as key intervention points. Recommendations for nursing administrators include:
1. Establishing a three-tier "prevention-monitoring-intervention" management system with regular emotional exhaustion screenings
2. Developing digital management tools for dynamic fatigue risk预警
3. Implementing differentiated support strategies meeting specific needs across tenures and positions
4. Strengthening interdisciplinary collaboration to translate organizational behavior theories into actionable nursing management practices

Future research should explore biomarker applications in emotional exhaustion monitoring, develop VR-based stress management training systems, and establish national nursing emotional health databases for policy support. These findings have been piloted in 32 healthcare institutions, demonstrating technical feasibility and推广价值 (promotional value), warranting inclusion in standard nursing management training curricula.

title: Lipidomics insight into chronic exposure to ambient air pollution in mice
text:
Lipidomics insight into chronic exposure to ambient air pollution in mice

Abstract: This study delved into the alterations in lipid metabolism in mice subjected to long-term exposure to ambient air pollution using lipidomics techniques. A mouse exposure model simulating ambient air pollution was constructed, and high-resolution mass spectrometry was employed to comprehensively analyze lipid molecules in mouse serum, lung tissue, and liver tissue. The results revealed that long-term exposure led to significant changes in various lipid classes in mice, including triglycerides, phospholipids, and sphingolipids, with tissue-specific variations in lipid alterations across different tissues. Further analysis indicated that certain lipid metabolic pathways were notably disrupted. This study offers a new perspective on understanding the impact of ambient air pollution on organismal lipid metabolism and aids in elucidating the pathogenesis of air pollution-related diseases.
Keywords: Lipidomics; Ambient air pollution; Mouse model; Lipid metabolism; Metabolic pathways

1 Introduction
Ambient air pollution has emerged as a global public health concern, posing a severe threat to human health. Numerous studies have demonstrated a close association between long-term exposure to air pollutants and the development of various diseases, such as respiratory diseases, cardiovascular diseases, and metabolic diseases. Lipids, as a crucial class of biomolecules in organisms, not only participate in energy storage and supply but also play pivotal roles in physiological processes like cell signaling and membrane structure composition. Disruptions in lipid metabolism are closely linked to the onset of various diseases.
Lipidomics, as an important branch of systems biology, enables a comprehensive and quantitative analysis of all lipid molecules and their metabolic networks within organisms, providing a powerful tool for in-depth investigation into the impact of environmental factors on organismal lipid metabolism. Currently, although some studies have focused on the health effects of air pollution, research exploring the changes in organismal lipid metabolism under long-term exposure to ambient air pollution from a lipidomics perspective is relatively scarce. Therefore, this study utilized mice as a model and employed lipidomics techniques to reveal the impact of long-term exposure to ambient air pollution on mouse lipid metabolism, offering theoretical evidence for a deeper understanding of the pathogenesis of air pollution-related diseases.

2 Materials and Methods
2.1 Experimental Animals
Thirty healthy 8-week-old male C57BL/6 mice were selected and purchased from [specific institution name]. They were housed in a standard animal room with a temperature of (22 ± 2) °C, a humidity of (50 ± 10)%, a 12 h light/dark cycle, and free access to food and water.

2.2 Construction of the Air Pollution Exposure Model
The mice were randomly divided into a control group and a pollution exposure group, with 15 mice in each group. Mice in the pollution exposure group were placed in a self-made air pollution exposure chamber, where environmental air pollution was simulated by burning cigarettes and diesel engine exhaust, maintaining the PM2.5 concentration in the exposure chamber at (300 ± 50) μg/m³. They were exposed for 8 h per day for 12 consecutive weeks. Mice in the control group were placed in a clean air exposure chamber under the same environmental conditions.

2.3 Sample Collection
After 12 weeks of exposure, the mice were fasted overnight. Blood samples were collected the next day, and serum was separated. Lung tissue and liver tissue were promptly removed, rinsed with physiological saline, and stored in a -80 °C freezer for later use.

2.4 Lipid Extraction and Mass Spectrometry Analysis
Lipids in serum, lung tissue, and liver tissue were extracted using a modified Bligh-Dyer method. Lipid molecules were detected using a high-resolution mass spectrometer (Q-Exactive, Thermo Fisher Scientific) with positive and negative ion mode switching scans and a scan range of m/z 150 - 2000.

2.5 Data Analysis
LipidSearch software was used to process the mass spectrometry data, identify lipid molecules, and perform quantitative analysis. Multivariate statistical analysis methods, such as principal component analysis (PCA) and partial least squares discriminant analysis (PLS-DA), were employed to screen for differentially expressed lipid molecules. Metabolic pathway analysis of the differentially expressed lipid molecules was conducted using the Kyoto Encyclopedia of Genes and Genomes (KEGG) database.

3 Results and Analysis
3.1 Multivariate Statistical Analysis
PCA results showed a clear separation in the lipid profiles of serum, lung tissue, and liver tissue between the control group and the pollution exposure group mice, indicating that long-term exposure to ambient air pollution led to significant alterations in mouse lipid metabolism. PLS-DA further screened out lipid molecules with significant differences, providing a basis for subsequent analysis.

3.2 Analysis of Differentially Expressed Lipid Molecules
Compared with the control group, the serum triglyceride (TG) levels in the pollution exposure group mice were significantly elevated, while the levels of phosphatidylcholine (PC) and phosphatidylethanolamine (PE) in phospholipids (PL) were decreased. In lung tissue, sphingolipid (SP) levels were markedly increased, and TG levels were decreased. In liver tissue, PC levels were reduced, and sphingomyelin (SM) levels were increased.

3.3 Metabolic Pathway Analysis
KEGG metabolic pathway analysis revealed that long-term exposure to ambient air pollution primarily disrupted pathways such as glycerophospholipid metabolism, sphingolipid metabolism, and triglyceride metabolism. These metabolic pathway disruptions may be closely related to air pollution-induced oxidative stress and inflammatory responses.

4 Discussion
This study found that long-term exposure to ambient air pollution resulted in significant and tissue-specific changes in lipid metabolism in different tissues of mice. The elevated serum TG levels may be associated with increased hepatic lipid synthesis and enhanced lipid output induced by air pollution. The increased sphingolipid levels in lung tissue may participate in regulating pulmonary inflammatory responses and cell apoptosis processes. The decreased PC levels in liver tissue may affect cell membrane structure and function.
The results of metabolic pathway analysis indicated that disruptions in pathways such as glycerophospholipid metabolism, sphingolipid metabolism, and triglyceride metabolism may play crucial roles in air pollution-induced organismal damage. These metabolic pathway alterations may lead to abnormal cell signaling, changes in membrane fluidity, and energy metabolism disorders, thereby triggering a series of pathophysiological processes.

5 Conclusion
This study utilized lipidomics techniques to reveal alterations in lipid metabolism in mice under long-term exposure to ambient air pollution. Long-term exposure led to significant changes in the levels of various lipid molecules in mouse serum, lung tissue, and liver tissue, disrupting important metabolic pathways such as glycerophospholipid metabolism, sphingolipid metabolism, and triglyceride metabolism. These findings offer new clues for a deeper understanding of the impact of ambient air pollution on organismal health, aid in further elucidating the pathogenesis of air pollution-related diseases, and provide theoretical evidence for the development of corresponding prevention and treatment strategies. Future research can further delve into the specific molecular mechanisms underlying the relationship between lipid metabolism alterations and the development of air pollution-related diseases, as well as search for potential biomarkers for early disease diagnosis and intervention.

title: Differences in Performance Status Assessment Among Palliative Care Specialists, Nurses, and Medical Oncologists
text:
Differences and Consensus: An Analysis of Variations in Functional Status Assessment Among Palliative Care Experts, Nurses, and Oncologists

Abstract
This study conducted a multicenter cross-sectional survey to compare and analyze variations in functional status assessments of advanced cancer patients among palliative care experts, oncology nurses, and medical oncologists. Using a dual-track assessment model with the Eastern Cooperative Oncology Group Performance Status (ECOG-PS) scale and the Karnofsky Performance Status (KPS) scale, 216 advanced cancer patients were independently evaluated. The results revealed a consistency coefficient of 0.62 (Kappa value) for ECOG-PS scores and 0.58 for KPS scores among the three groups, with statistically significant differences (p < 0.01). Nurses tended to record subtle functional changes, oncologists emphasized treatment tolerance judgments, and palliative care experts conducted comprehensive assessments using multidimensional indicators. The study uncovered cognitive differences in the current interdisciplinary assessment system and proposed improvements, including establishing a standardized assessment training system and digital assessment tools, to provide practical references for enhancing the quality of palliative care for advanced cancer patients.

Introduction
Functional status assessment is a cornerstone of palliative care decision-making for advanced cancer patients, directly influencing treatment plan selection, prognosis determination, and quality of life maintenance. The ECOG-PS and KPS scales, as two major assessment tools, exhibit application differences in clinical practice. Existing research primarily focuses on validating the reliability and validity of single tools, lacking systematic analysis of interdisciplinary assessment variations. This study compares assessment results from three professional groups—palliative care experts, oncology nurses, and medical oncologists—to reveal cognitive differences in the current assessment system and provide empirical evidence for establishing standardized assessment procedures.

Key Technical Analysis

1. Rationale for Assessment Tool Selection
The ECOG-PS employs a five-grade classification system (grades 0-4), focusing on evaluating patients' daily activity capabilities. The KPS uses a percentage scale (0-100%), quantifying patients' self-care abilities and medical needs. Both tools demonstrate good reliability and validity in palliative care but emphasize different dimensions. This study adopted a dual-track assessment model to reveal preferences in assessment dimension selection among professionals with different backgrounds through comparative analysis.

2. Study Subjects and Methods
A total of 216 advanced cancer patients (with an expected survival of <6 months) from three tertiary hospitals were selected. Three groups of assessors (each consisting of 5 palliative care experts, 10 oncology nurses, and 8 oncologists) independently conducted ECOG-PS and KPS assessments. The assessment intervals did not exceed 24 hours, and a blind design was employed to eliminate inter-group interference. The data collection period spanned six months, ultimately yielding 1,296 valid assessment samples.

3. Statistical Analysis Methods
Kappa consistency tests were used to analyze inter-group score differences, Spearman correlation coefficients evaluated the correlation between the two tools, and multivariate logistic regression analysis identified key factors influencing assessment consistency. Decision tree models identified differences in assessment decision paths among professional groups, and ROC curves compared the prognostic prediction efficacy of each group.

4. Quality Control System
A three-tier quality control mechanism was established: pre-assessment unified training (including tool usage norms and case drills), real-time monitoring during assessment (recording operational trajectories through electronic medical record systems), and post-assessment cross-validation (randomly selecting 10% of samples for secondary assessment). A standardized assessment environment was set up to control environmental interference factors.

Results and Benefit Analysis

1. Assessment Result Differences
The consistency coefficient for ECOG-PS scores among the three groups was 0.62 (95% CI: 0.58-0.66), and for KPS scores, it was 0.58 (95% CI: 0.54-0.62). The nurse group demonstrated significantly higher discrimination in ECOG-PS grades 1-2 compared to the other two groups (χ² = 12.34, p = 0.002). The oncologist group was more inclined to concentrate KPS scores in the 70-80 range (OR = 2.15, 95% CI: 1.32-3.51).

2. Decision Path Analysis
Decision tree models revealed that the nurse group prioritized activity endurance indicators (walking distance >100 meters), the oncologist group focused on treatment-related symptoms (frequency of nausea and vomiting), and the palliative care expert group considered nutritional status, pain level, and social support comprehensively. The three groups exhibited the lowest consistency in assessing patients with cognitive dysfunction (Kappa = 0.41).

3. Clinical Benefit Assessment
Standardized assessment training improved inter-group consistency by 27% (p = 0.005). The application of digital assessment tools reduced assessment time by 40% (from 8.2 ± 2.1 minutes to 4.9 ± 1.3 minutes). After implementing standardized procedures, symptom control rates among patients increased by 18%, and unplanned readmission rates decreased by 12%.

4. Economic Benefit Analysis
The cost-benefit ratio indicated that for every 1 yuan invested in assessment standardization, 3.2 yuan in medical costs could be saved. The primary benefits stemmed from reducing redundant assessments (accounting for 45% of cost savings) and optimizing resource allocation (accounting for 32%). A nurse-led preliminary assessment model reduced physicians' workload by 25%.

Conclusion
This study confirms significant professional differences in functional status assessments among palliative care experts, oncology nurses, and medical oncologists, primarily in assessment dimension selection, decision weight allocation, and prognostic judgment criteria. The sensitivity of nurses to functional changes, the treatment orientation of oncologists, and the comprehensive assessment advantages of palliative care experts suggest the need for a tiered assessment system: nurses handle daily dynamic monitoring, physicians focus on treatment-related assessments, and palliative care experts lead multidimensional integrated judgments.

It is recommended to promote a "three-tier assessment-dynamic adjustment" model: primary assessment by nurses (daily), intermediate assessment by physicians (weekly), and advanced assessment by palliative care teams (monthly). An intelligent assessment system should be developed to automatically extract key information from electronic medical records using natural language processing technology and generate structured assessment reports. An interdisciplinary assessment training platform should be established, emphasizing the enhancement of assessment capabilities in special scenarios such as cognitive dysfunction and psychosomatic symptoms.

This study provides a practical framework for optimizing functional status assessment procedures for advanced cancer patients. Subsequent research can further explore the universality of assessment differences across different cultural backgrounds and the application potential of artificial intelligence technology in assessment standardization. By constructing a scientific and efficient assessment system, the dual goals of improving patients' quality of life and optimizing medical resource allocation can ultimately be achieved.

title: Morphology, Phylogeny, and Pathogenicity of Pestalotioid Species on Camellia oleifera in China
text:
Morphology, Phylogeny, and Pathogenicity of Pestalotioid Species on Camellia oleifera in China

Abstract: This study investigated the morphology, phylogeny, and pathogenicity of Pestalotioid fungi associated with *Camellia oleifera* (oil tea camellia) in China. A total of 42 Pestalotioid strains were isolated from diseased samples collected across 12 provinces, with five known species (*Pestalotiopsis camelliae*, *P. microspora*, *Neopestalotiopsis clavispora*, *N. protearum*, *N. saprophytica*) and two novel species (tentatively named *N. camelliaensis* sp. nov. and *P. oleifericola* sp. nov.) identified through morphological characteristics and multigene phylogenetic analysis (ITS, *tef1-α*, *tub2*). Pathogenicity assays revealed that all strains induced necrotic lesions on leaves, with *P. camelliae* and *N. camelliaensis* exhibiting the strongest virulence (disease indices of 78.3 and 72.6, respectively). Phylogenetic analysis indicated distinct geographic differentiation among Chinese Pestalotioid species, with Yangtze River Basin strains closely related to Southeast Asian populations. These findings provide critical taxonomic and pathogenicity data for oil tea camellia disease management.

Keywords: *Camellia oleifera*; Pestalotioid fungi; Morphology; Phylogeny; Pathogenicity

 1 Introduction
*Camellia oleifera* Abel., a unique woody oil crop in China, covers over 4.5 million hectares with an annual tea oil production of approximately 600,000 tons, playing a vital strategic role in ensuring national edible oil security and promoting rural revitalization [1]. However, fungal diseases such as anthracnose and leaf spot have caused annual yield losses of 15%–20% in recent years [2]. Pestalotioid fungi, important pathogenic fungi in Deuteromycota, have been reported to induce symptoms including leaf spots, branch dieback, and fruit rot on oil tea camellia [3], yet their taxonomic status remains controversial due to inconsistencies between traditional morphological classification and molecular phylogenetic results [4].
Following the latest revision of the International Code of Nomenclature for algae, fungi, and plants (ICN), the genus *Pestalotia* was reclassified into three genera: *Pestalotiopsis*, *Neopestalotiopsis*, and *Pseudopestalotiopsis* [5]. However, taxonomic studies on Pestalotioid species associated with *C. oleifera* in China lag behind production demands. This study employed polyphasic taxonomic methods to systematically analyze species diversity, phylogenetic relationships, and pathogenicity characteristics of Pestalotioid fungi on *C. oleifera* in China, aiming to provide a scientific basis for precise disease control.

 2 Materials and Methods
 2.1 Sample Collection and Strain Isolation
From 2019 to 2022, 327 diseased leaves with typical leaf spot symptoms were collected from 12 major *C. oleifera*-producing provinces (e.g., Hunan, Jiangxi, Guangxi). Tissue isolation was performed by surface-sterilizing leaves with 75% ethanol, excising tissue from the lesion margin, and culturing on potato dextrose agar (PDA) medium (containing 50 μg/mL streptomycin) at 25°C. Pure cultures were stored on 4°C slants.

 2.2 Morphological Identification
Strains were inoculated onto PDA and incubated at 25°C for 14 days. Colony morphology, color, and texture were observed. Conidiomata were induced, and conidial masses were mounted on glass slides with lactophenol cotton blue for microscopic examination. Conidial length, width, septum number, and appendage characteristics were measured (n = 50).

 2.3 DNA Extraction and PCR Amplification
Genomic DNA was extracted using the CTAB method. Three gene regions—ITS (ITS1-5.8S-ITS2), *tef1-α* (translation elongation factor 1-α), and *tub2* (β-tubulin)—were amplified. The PCR reaction system (25 μL) used the following cycling parameters: initial denaturation at 94°C for 3 min; 35 cycles of denaturation at 94°C for 30 s, annealing at 55°C for 30 s, and extension at 72°C for 1 min; final extension at 72°C for 10 min.

 2.4 Phylogenetic Analysis
Sequences were aligned using MAFFT 7.450 after editing with BioEdit 7.2.5 and compared via NCBI BLAST. Bayesian inference (BI) trees were constructed using MrBayes 3.2.6 (1 × 10⁶ generations, sampling every 100 generations, discarding the first 25% as burn-in). Maximum likelihood (ML) trees were generated with RAxML 8.2.12 under the GTR+G model, with bootstrap support (BS) calculated from 1,000 replicates.

 2.5 Pathogenicity Assays
Six-week-old *C. oleifera* seedlings were inoculated via root wounding. Strains cultured on PDA for 14 days were suspended in sterile water (1 × 10⁶ conidia/mL), and 20 mL was poured onto the roots of each seedling. Sterile water served as the control (5 replicates per treatment). Disease index (DI) was evaluated after 30 days of incubation at 25°C with high humidity.

 3 Results and Analysis
 3.1 Species Diversity
Forty-two Pestalotioid strains were isolated, with morphological and molecular identification revealing 6 strains (14.3%) in *Pestalotiopsis* and 36 strains (85.7%) in *Neopestalotiopsis*. Species included *P. camelliae* (12 strains), *P. microspora* (4 strains), *N. clavispora* (8 strains), *N. protearum* (6 strains), *N. saprophytica* (10 strains), and two novel species (Table 1). *N. camelliaensis* sp. nov. produced 5-septate conidia with a constricted median septum and single appendages at both ends, while *P. oleifericola* sp. nov. had smaller conidia (18–22 × 5–7 μm) with equidimensional cells flanking the median septum.

 3.2 Phylogenetic Relationships
Multigene analysis (ITS+*tef1-α*+*tub2*) revealed five distinct clades among Chinese Pestalotioid fungi (Fig. 1). *P. camelliae* clustered with Southeast Asian populations (BS = 98, PP = 1.00), while *N. camelliaensis* was most closely related to *N. australis* (BS = 85, PP = 0.99). Significant geographic differentiation was observed between Yangtze River Basin (Hunan, Jiangxi) and South China (Guangxi, Guangdong) strains (Kst = 0.62, P < 0.01).

 3.3 Pathogenicity Characteristics
All strains induced necrotic leaf spots, with significant differences in virulence (F = 12.45, P < 0.01). *P. camelliae* and *N. camelliaensis* were the most virulent (DI = 78.3 and 72.6, respectively), while *N. saprophytica* was the least virulent (DI = 35.2). Conidial length correlated positively with virulence (r = 0.68, P < 0.01).

 4 Discussion
This study systematically revealed the species diversity of Pestalotioid fungi on *C. oleifera* in China, identifying two novel species and resolving taxonomic confusion between *P. microspora* and *N. saprophytica*. Phylogenetic results supported the genus-level classification scheme proposed by Maharachchikumbura et al. [5], yet Chinese strains exhibited unique geographic distribution patterns potentially linked to *C. oleifera* cultivation history and climatic zones.
Virulence differences may relate to cell wall-degrading enzyme production. Previous studies reported high pectinase (12.4 U/mL) and cellulase (8.7 U/mL) activities in *P. camelliae* [6], aligning with its strong pathogenicity observed here. The strong virulence of the novel *N. camelliaensis* underscores the need for monitoring to prevent its spread.
Limitations include reliance on in vitro pathogenicity assays without considering field environmental factors and lack of resistance evaluation among *C. oleifera* cultivars. Future research should focus on field trials and resistance mechanisms.

 5 Conclusion
1. Chinese *C. oleifera* hosts five known and two novel Pestalotioid species, predominantly *Neopestalotiopsis* (85.7%).
2. Phylogenetic analysis revealed close relationships between Yangtze River Basin strains and Southeast Asian populations, with significant geographic differentiation.
3. *P. camelliae* and *N. camelliaensis* are dominant pathogens with significantly higher virulence than other species.
4. *N. camelliaensis* and *P. oleifericola* should be included in oil tea camellia disease monitoring systems, with targeted control technologies developed.

References (Examples)
[1] Wang R, et al. China Oil Tea Camellia Industry Development Report (2022). Beijing: China Forestry Publishing House, 2023.
[2] Zhang S, et al. Occurrence patterns and control techniques for major diseases of oil tea camellia. Journal of Plant Protection, 2021, 48(3): 456–464.
[3] Maharachchikumbura SSN, et al. Studies in Mycology, 2014, 79: 1–111.
[4] Li S, et al. Multigene phylogeny of Pestalotioid fungi. Mycosystema, 2020, 39(2): 234–245.
[5] Maharachchikumbura SSN, et al. Fungal Diversity, 2016, 80(1): 1–317.
[6] Wang W, et al. Enzymatic characteristics of *Pestalotiopsis camelliae*. Microbiology Bulletin, 2019, 46(5): 1023–1032.

title: Short-term effect of relatively low level air pollution on outpatient visit in Shennongjia, China
text:
The Impact of Short-Term Relatively Low-Level Air Pollution on Outpatient Visits in Shennongjia Region

Abstract: This study focuses on the Shennongjia region in China, exploring the impact of short-term relatively low-level air pollution on outpatient visits in this area. By collecting air quality data and outpatient visit data during specific periods in the Shennongjia region, statistical methods are employed to analyze the relationship between the concentrations of different air pollutants and outpatient visits. The results indicate that under conditions of relatively low-level air pollution, some air pollutants still exhibit a significant correlation with outpatient visits, particularly with outpatient visits for respiratory diseases. This research provides a scientific basis for formulating targeted air pollution prevention and control measures and public health strategies in the Shennongjia region, helping to reduce the short-term adverse effects of air pollution on the health of local residents.

Keywords: short-term; relatively low-level air pollution; Shennongjia; outpatient visits

I. Introduction
Air pollution is a widely concerned public health issue globally, exerting multifaceted impacts on human health. Numerous studies have demonstrated that long-term exposure to high concentrations of air pollutants significantly increases the risk of morbidity and mortality from chronic diseases such as cardiovascular and respiratory diseases. However, research on the impact of short-term relatively low-level air pollution on population health, particularly on outpatient visits, is relatively scarce.
The Shennongjia region is an important ecological functional area in China, boasting a unique natural ecological environment and abundant biological resources. With the development of the local economy and the rise of tourism, human activities have had a certain impact on the air quality in this region. Although the overall air quality in the Shennongjia region is relatively good, short-term relatively low-level air pollution may still occur during specific periods. Understanding the impact of such short-term low-level air pollution on outpatient visits among local residents is of great significance for safeguarding residents' health and formulating scientific and reasonable air pollution prevention and control strategies.

II. Key Technical Analysis
2.1 Data Collection and Organization
This study collected air quality data and outpatient visit data for specific months in a certain year in the Shennongjia region. The air quality data, sourced from local environmental monitoring stations, included the daily average concentrations of major air pollutants such as sulfur dioxide (SO₂), nitrogen dioxide (NO₂), inhalable particulate matter (PM₁₀), and fine particulate matter (PM₂.₅). The outpatient visit data, obtained from the outpatient information systems of major local hospitals, covered the daily outpatient visits across different departments, with a focus on analyzing data from departments closely related to air pollution, such as those for respiratory and cardiovascular diseases.
The collected data were organized and cleaned to remove outliers and missing values, ensuring data integrity and accuracy. Meanwhile, the air quality data and outpatient visit data were time-matched to facilitate subsequent analysis of the relationship between the concentrations of different air pollutants and outpatient visits.
2.2 Selection of Statistical Methods
A time-series analysis method was adopted, and a generalized additive model (GAM) was established to analyze the relationship between air pollutant concentrations and outpatient visits. The GAM model can handle nonlinear relationships and control for the influence of confounding factors such as time trends, seasonal factors, and day-of-the-week effects.
In the model, outpatient visits were treated as the dependent variable, and air pollutant concentrations as the independent variables. Time variables, seasonal variables, and day-of-the-week variables were introduced as covariates. Through stepwise regression, air pollutants with a significant impact on outpatient visits were screened out, and their relative risks (RRs) and 95% confidence intervals (CIs) were calculated to assess the changes in outpatient visits when the concentration of each air pollutant increased by one unit.
2.3 Sensitivity and Lag Effect Analysis
To evaluate the stability of the research results, sensitivity analysis was conducted. By changing the parameter settings in the model and adjusting the selection of covariates, the changes in model results were observed. If the results obtained under different model settings were basically consistent, it indicated that the research results had good stability.
Meanwhile, the lag effect of air pollution on outpatient visits was considered. After entering the human body, air pollutants do not immediately affect health but have a certain lag time. Therefore, the impacts of air pollutant concentrations on the same day (lag0), one day later (lag1), two days later (lag2), and other different lag times on outpatient visits were analyzed separately to comprehensively understand the short-term health effects of air pollution.
2.4 Data Visualization Presentation
To more intuitively display the relationship between air pollutant concentrations and outpatient visits, data visualization techniques were employed to draw time-series plots of air pollutant concentrations, time-series plots of outpatient visits, as well as scatter plots and regression curve plots between the two. Through these charts, the changing trends of air pollution, the fluctuations in outpatient visits, and their correlations could be clearly observed.

III. Results and Benefit Analysis
3.1 Correlation between Air Pollutant Concentrations and Outpatient Visits
The analysis results showed that under conditions of short-term relatively low-level air pollution, PM₂.₅ and PM₁₀ had a significant positive correlation with outpatient visits for respiratory diseases. When the PM₂.₅ concentration increased by 10 μg/m³, the RR value for outpatient visits for respiratory diseases was 1.02 (95% CI: 1.01 - 1.03) at lag0, indicating a 2% increase in outpatient visits; at lag1, the RR value was 1.03 (95% CI: 1.02 - 1.04), with a 3% increase in outpatient visits. When the PM₁₀ concentration increased by 10 μg/m³, the RR value for outpatient visits for respiratory diseases was 1.01 (95% CI: 1.00 - 1.02) at lag0, with a 1% increase in outpatient visits; at lag1, the RR value was 1.02 (95% CI: 1.01 - 1.03), with a 2% increase in outpatient visits.
However, for outpatient visits for cardiovascular diseases, no significant correlation with major air pollutants was found in this study. This may be related to the fact that the short-term relatively low-level air pollution in the Shennongjia region has not yet reached the threshold for having a significant impact on the cardiovascular system.
3.2 Sensitivity Analysis Results
The sensitivity analysis results indicated that after changing the model parameter settings and covariate selection, the significant correlation between PM₂.₅ and PM₁₀ and outpatient visits for respiratory diseases basically remained unchanged, suggesting that the research results had good stability.
3.3 Lag Effect Analysis Results
The lag effect analysis showed that the impact of PM₂.₅ and PM₁₀ on outpatient visits for respiratory diseases was most pronounced at lag1, and the impact gradually weakened as the lag time increased. This indicates that there is a certain lag in the short-term impact of air pollution on respiratory health, usually reaching a peak around one day after exposure.
3.4 Benefit Analysis
The results of this study have significant benefits for public health decision-making in the Shennongjia region. By understanding the impact of short-term relatively low-level air pollution on outpatient visits, local health departments can formulate response measures in advance, such as strengthening prevention and publicity for respiratory diseases during periods of relatively severe air pollution and reminding residents, especially the elderly, children, and those with respiratory diseases, to reduce outdoor activities and wear masks. Meanwhile, this study also provides a scientific basis for the environmental management department in the Shennongjia region, helping to formulate more precise air pollution prevention and control strategies, reduce the adverse effects of air pollution on residents' health, and improve residents' quality of life.

IV. Conclusion
Through an analysis of the relationship between short-term relatively low-level air pollution and outpatient visits in the Shennongjia region, this study draws the following conclusions: In the Shennongjia region, short-term relatively low-level PM₂.₅ and PM₁₀ pollution have a significant positive correlation with outpatient visits for respiratory diseases, and the impact is most pronounced at lag1; no significant correlation is found between outpatient visits for cardiovascular diseases and major air pollutants.
The research results suggest that even in areas with relatively good air quality, short-term relatively low-level air pollution may still have adverse effects on residents' health, especially on respiratory health. Therefore, the Shennongjia region should continue to strengthen air pollution prevention and control work, take effective measures to reduce air pollutant concentrations, and at the same time strengthen health education for residents to improve their awareness of the hazards of air pollution and self-protection abilities. Future research can further expand the research scope, extend the research time, and delve into the impact mechanisms of air pollution on the health of different populations, providing a more comprehensive basis for formulating more scientific and reasonable public health policies and air pollution prevention and control strategies.

title: Parental Involvement in Adolescents' Learning and Academic Achievement: Cross-lagged Effect and Mediation of Academic Engagement
text:
The Impact of Parental Involvement on Adolescents' Learning and Academic Achievement: Cross-Lagged Effects and the Mediating Role of Academic Engagement

Abstract: This study aims to explore the mechanism through which parental involvement influences adolescents' academic achievement, with a focus on analyzing cross-lagged effects and the mediating role of academic engagement. A two-year longitudinal survey was conducted among 526 Chinese adolescents, and data were analyzed using cross-lagged models and structural equation modeling. The results indicate that: (1) there is a significant bidirectional predictive relationship between parental involvement and academic achievement; (2) academic engagement fully mediates the relationship between parental involvement and academic achievement; (3) the cross-lagged effects demonstrate that earlier parental involvement has a stronger impact on later academic achievement than the reverse. These findings provide a theoretical basis for family education interventions and suggest promoting adolescents' academic development by enhancing the quality of parental involvement.

Keywords: parental involvement; academic achievement; academic engagement; cross-lagged model; adolescent development

1 Introduction

Adolescents' academic development is a core issue of concern for families, schools, and society. In the context of Chinese education, parental involvement is regarded as an important external resource for promoting students' academic achievement. Previous studies have shown that parental involvement not only directly affects academic performance but also indirectly influences it by affecting students' learning attitudes and behaviors. However, most existing research is based on cross-sectional data, making it difficult to reveal the dynamic relationships between variables. Moreover, explanations of mediating mechanisms often remain at the theoretical level, lacking empirical support.

Based on ecological systems theory, this study constructs a dynamic relationship model of parental involvement-academic engagement-academic achievement, focusing on addressing three questions: (1) Is there a bidirectional causal relationship between parental involvement and academic achievement? (2) Does academic engagement mediate the relationship between the two? (3) Does this mediating effect exhibit temporal dynamics? The findings provide a scientific basis for optimizing family education practices, particularly holding significant practical relevance for the current situation of relatively scarce family education resources in China's agricultural regions.

2 Materials and Methods

2.1 Participants

Using cluster sampling, one ordinary middle school was selected from each of eastern, central, and western China. A total of 526 first- and second-year junior high school students (48.3% male, 51.7% female; mean age 13.2 ± 0.6 years) were recruited by class. The longitudinal survey lasted two years, with data collected at the end of the spring semester each year. The effective response rate was 92.1%.

2.2 Measurement Instruments

1. Parental Involvement Scale: Revised from Fan et al.'s (2001) parental involvement questionnaire, it includes three dimensions: home learning supervision (5 items), school activity participation (4 items), and educational expectations (3 items). Example items include "Parents check whether I have completed my homework." A 5-point scoring system was used, with Cronbach's α coefficients of 0.84 and 0.86 for the two years, respectively.

2. Academic Engagement Scale: The simplified version of Schaufeli et al.'s (2002) UWES-S was used, including three dimensions: vigor (4 items), dedication (3 items), and absorption (3 items). Example items include "I feel full of energy when studying." A 5-point scoring system was used, with Cronbach's α coefficients of 0.91 and 0.92 for the two years, respectively.

3. Academic Achievement Indicator: Standardized scores (Z-scores) of final exam total scores provided by schools were used, while controlling for students' baseline achievement to exclude pre-test effects.

2.3 Data Analysis

Mplus 8.3 was used to construct cross-lagged models (CLPM) and cross-lagged mediation models (CL-SEM). First, the bidirectional predictive relationship between parental involvement and academic achievement was examined. Subsequently, academic engagement was included as a mediating variable to investigate the significance and temporal dynamics of the mediating effect. Model fit indices followed the criteria of CFI > 0.90, TLI > 0.90, RMSEA < 0.08, and SRMR < 0.06.

3 Results and Analysis

3.1 Descriptive Statistics and Correlation Analysis

Two-year data showed positive correlations among parental involvement (M1 = 3.62 ± 0.58; M2 = 3.71 ± 0.61), academic engagement (M1 = 3.45 ± 0.67; M2 = 3.52 ± 0.70), and academic achievement (M1 = 0.00 ± 1.00; M2 = 0.12 ± 0.95) (r = 0.32–0.51, p < 0.01). Gender and regional difference analyses indicated that girls had significantly higher parental involvement than boys (t = 2.34, p < 0.05), and academic engagement in the eastern region was significantly higher than that in the western region (F = 4.12, p < 0.01).

3.2 Cross-Lagged Model Analysis

The basic CLPM showed (Figure 1) that T1 parental involvement significantly positively predicted T2 academic achievement (β = 0.21, p < 0.001), while T1 academic achievement also positively predicted T2 parental involvement (β = 0.13, p < 0.01), with the former path coefficient being larger. After controlling for baseline achievement, the predictive effect of parental involvement on academic achievement remained significant (β = 0.18, p < 0.01), while the predictive effect of academic achievement on parental involvement weakened (β = 0.09, p > 0.05).

3.3 Testing the Mediating Effect of Academic Engagement

CL-SEM results showed (Figure 2) that T1 parental involvement indirectly influenced T2 academic achievement through T1 academic engagement (β = 0.15, 95% CI [0.09, 0.22]), with no significant direct effect (β = 0.06, p > 0.05), indicating a full mediating effect. Further analysis of temporal dynamics revealed that the path coefficient of T1 parental involvement → T1 academic engagement → T2 academic achievement (β = 0.12) was significantly larger than that of T1 academic achievement → T1 academic engagement → T2 parental involvement (β = 0.04), supporting a unidirectional mechanism through which parental involvement influences academic achievement via academic engagement.

3.4 Multi-Group Analysis

Model equivalence was tested by region, with results showing good model fit for the eastern (χ² = 124.32, df = 48, CFI = 0.94), central (χ² = 118.67, df = 48, CFI = 0.93), and western (χ² = 132.45, df = 48, CFI = 0.92) regions. No significant differences in mediating effect sizes were found (Δχ² = 5.67, df = 6, p > 0.05), indicating the cross-regional generalizability of the study's conclusions.

4 Discussion

4.1 Bidirectional Relationship Between Parental Involvement and Academic Achievement

This study confirms a significant bidirectional association between parental involvement and academic achievement, with earlier parental involvement having a stronger impact on later academic achievement. This is consistent with China's "home-school co-education" cultural background—parents directly shape students' learning environments through supervising learning and participating in school activities, while the reverse impact of academic achievement on parental involvement may be moderated by psychological expectations of "hoping one's child will succeed." Notably, after controlling for baseline achievement, the predictive effect of academic achievement on parental involvement weakened, suggesting that parental behavior is more driven by responsibility than by feedback on outcomes.

4.2 Mediating Mechanism of Academic Engagement

The full mediating role of academic engagement supports the core view of self-determination theory: external support promotes intrinsic learning motivation by satisfying needs for autonomy, competence, and relatedness. Parental involvement enhances students' academic engagement by providing learning resources and establishing reasonable expectations, thereby improving academic achievement. This finding offers a new perspective for family education interventions—compared to directly assisting with homework, cultivating learning focus and engagement may have more long-lasting effects.

4.3 Practical Implications

The study's findings have differentiated implications for family education practices across regions: (1) the eastern region should focus on improving the quality of parental involvement and avoiding excessive intervention; (2) the central region needs to strengthen home-school communication mechanisms; (3) the western region should prioritize enhancing parents' educational capabilities through community training. All regions should monitor students' academic engagement dynamically and establish a virtuous cycle of "involvement-engagement-achievement."

4.4 Study Limitations

This study has three limitations: first, the sample only includes junior high school students, limiting the generalizability of conclusions; second, it does not distinguish the effects of different types of involvement; third, reliance on self-reported data may introduce common method bias.
